name: litellm

facts.description: The fastest, litest AI Gateway. Rust core with Python SDK. Call 100+ LLM APIs in OpenAI (or native) format with cost tracking, guardrails, load balancing, and logging [Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenAI, VertexAI, vLLM, Nvidia NIM]

title: LiteLLM: A Unified Gateway for Calling and Governing LLM APIs
answer: LiteLLM is an open source AI gateway from BerriAI that lets Python code and a proxy server call over 100 LLM APIs in OpenAI or native format, with cost tracking, guardrails, load balancing and logging. It sits between your application and providers such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, Azure and Vertex AI. The one thing to know before adopting it is that it is a fast-moving operational dependency: the project has shipped breaking regressions and incident reports, so pin versions and read release notes.

sections.body: LiteLLM is made by BerriAI and distributed from the repository BerriAI/litellm under a custom licence. It is a Python library and an accompanying proxy server, described on its official site as the fastest, litest AI gateway, with a Rust core and a Python SDK. It appeared as a way to call more than 100 LLM APIs in OpenAI or native format, and the site lists Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, Vertex AI, vLLM and Nvidia NIM among the providers it covers. In the AI stack it occupies the gateway layer: it does not train models or serve weights itself, it sits between application code and model providers, normalising requests, routing them, and recording what they cost. The repository shows a last push in October 2026 and roughly 60,000 stars, so it is an actively maintained project rather than a frozen utility.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The concrete jobs LiteLLM does are model routing and load balancing across providers, cost tracking and spend attribution, guardrails, logging, and reliability testing. Its tutorials show batch_completion_models_all_responses sending one conversation to every model in parallel and returning only the responses that succeeded, which makes it useful for comparing providers, and load_test_model for driving concurrent requests against a single model. The proxy adds budgets and rate limits at the key, team, agent and customer level, and the site describes an Agent Gateway, a Model Gateway and an MCP Gateway under one control plane, with per-user attribution passed through headers such as X-LiteLLM-User-Id and X-LiteLLM-Team-Id. It is strongest where a team needs one consistent interface to many providers, central spend visibility, and the ability to swap models without rewriting application code. It is not a training framework, and nothing on the site claims it is the best choice for model development itself.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: The library side is approachable for anyone who already writes Python and has called an LLM API, because the point of the project is to keep the OpenAI request shape while changing the model string. The proxy side asks for more: you need to understand deployment, Redis, authentication through OIDC or another supported credential, and the budget and rate limit model before running it in front of production traffic. The official site offers tutorials, a blog with incident reports, and documentation of the gateway features, which is enough for a beginner to make a first call but not a substitute for systems knowledge once you operate the proxy. The site does not present a structured course or a mathematics prerequisite, and it does not claim the project is suitable for people with no programming background.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: LiteLLM is written in Python and integrates with the major commercial and self-hosted model providers named on its site, including Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, Vertex AI, vLLM and Nvidia NIM. Around the core library the project documents an Agent Gateway that speaks the A2A JSON-RPC interface, an MCP Gateway that centralises tool access and upstream authentication, and admin surfaces including a Slack admin agent called LiteAdmin built on a management API connector. The blog carries tags for ai-gateway and incident-report, with twelve and fourteen posts respectively, which shows a project that publishes both feature work and postmortems. Community scale is visible in the repository star count, and the documentation site itself is the primary support surface. The facts available do not include a count of contributors or a survey of third-party plugins, so the breadth of the wider ecosystem beyond what the site documents cannot be stated here.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: LiteLLM is built for both, but the two halves have different costs. For prototyping, the Python SDK lets you point existing OpenAI-style code at a new provider by changing a model name, and the batch and load testing helpers make provider comparison quick. For production, the project has been migrating its hot path to Rust, and its own benchmark claims the Rust gateway serves about 15 times the throughput of the Python proxy, 453 to 6,782 requests per second, on about 11 times less memory, 359MB down to 32MB, with per-request overhead falling from about 7.5ms to about 0.05ms. The site commits to sub-1ms overhead and a sub-100MB binary. The cost of that performance work is churn: the Rust gateway was in early beta at the time of writing, and the Python proxy remains the mature path, so teams choosing the fast path are adopting something still being finished.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The site describes enterprise customers running the proxy behind nginx in Kubernetes, with SSO and SAML, audit logs, spend tracking, multi-team management and guardrails described as built for production. The incident reports reference an enterprise customer with a proxy fleet and teams tracking daily spend, which indicates real operational use rather than hobby adoption. LiteLLM is a current standard in the narrow sense that it is a widely starred, actively developed gateway, and the site treats it as the layer customers rely on so they do not have to track provider quirks themselves. It is not presented as a legacy choice. For someone choosing what to learn, the transferable skills are gateway operations, provider abstraction, budget and identity management, and reading release notes carefully, since the project's own reports show that version discipline matters here.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: LiteLLM is a Python project with a Rust core, and it is typically used alongside whatever language and framework the application is already written in, because the proxy exposes an HTTP interface that any client can call. In a polyglot stack it belongs in the same position as other gateways, sitting in front of model providers and behind application services, and the site benchmarks it directly against Portkey, Bifrost and its own Python proxy. It complements rather than replaces inference servers such as vLLM, which it can route to, and agent frameworks, whose calls it can govern through the Agent Gateway and MCP Gateway. The pattern it belongs to is the one where a single control plane handles authentication, routing, budgets and logging while the application stays unaware of which provider ultimately answers.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: The project's own incident reports are the clearest statement of its limits. A defect in v1.100.0 caused kernel OOM kills and thousands of 502s for one enterprise customer when provider failures and an unreachable Redis coincided, with a single allocation reaching 27GB, and the fix was not backported before that version was tagged stable. A separate regression in v1.91.0 and v1.91.1 silently broke Anthropic prompt caching for Claude Code on Bedrock, cutting cache hit rates from roughly 90% to 25 to 45% and raising spend two to three times while requests still returned 200s. The Rust gateway was in early beta, and the site says the migration is ongoing, so its performance claims are the project's own benchmark rather than independent results. The official material does not say how long the Python proxy will be maintained alongside the Rust server, does not give a support policy for older versions, and does not publish an independent security audit. The licence is listed as custom, and the facts available do not explain its terms.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
